script.opening: "Hello, I've just registered with you — I moved here last week. Look, I'm on methadone, 60ml a day, and my script runs out today. If I don't get it I'll be climbing the walls by tonight and honestly I'm scared I'll end up using again. I just need you to write me a methadone script now, today. Please, I can't be without it."

facts.text: On methadone for three years with the Leeds drug service, 60 ml once a day, supervised at the pharmacy at first, now picking up twice a week. Last dose collected yesterday — "that was my last one".
Your keyworker is Sam at "Forward Leeds"; you have the number on your phone. Pharmacy: Boots on Kirkstall Road. You will happily give consent for the doctor to call them.
"I moved in a hurry — my mum got ill and I came to look after her. I didn't sort the transfer. Stupid, I know."
Clean from heroin for 18 months. No other drugs. No benzodiazepines or alcohol to excess. Urine tests at the old service were clean.
Hepatitis C treated two years ago. No other medicines. No allergies. You do not have naloxone with you — "it's in a drawer back in Leeds".

35, staying with your mum, who has just had a stroke. You were working part-time in a warehouse in Leeds. Your daughter (8) lives with her mum in Leeds and you see her at weekends — "I'm not losing that again".
Anxious and pressured, fear of withdrawal and, more, of relapse: "If I score once, that's it."

Polite but urgent; you will push for a script "just for today". If the doctor refuses outright and offers nothing, get desperate: "So I'm just meant to go and score then?" If they explain why they cannot safely prescribe without checking, but promise to ring your old service and the local drug service today and keep you safe meanwhile, you accept, give consent and contact details, and agree a time to be called back.

ice.ideas: "A GP can just write me a methadone script today."
ice.concerns: "I'm scared I'll end up using again." And losing contact with your daughter.
ice.expectations: "Write me a script now." You will accept an urgent verification and same-day plan if you are not left with nothing.

cues: "I'm scared I'll end up using again." — say in the opening.
"My keyworker's number is on my phone." — say when the doctor talks about checking.
"I'm not losing my little girl again." — say if asked about family or what keeps you going.

checkpoints.text: Does NOT prescribe methadone blind on an unverified phone request — recognising the fatal overdose risk of an unverified/excessive dose or lost tolerance — while also NOT simply refusing and abandoning him to withdrawal/relapse
Acts with genuine URGENCY to VERIFY: contacts his previous drug service/prescriber and dispensing pharmacy to confirm the dose, regimen and last pick-up

Routes him rapidly to the LOCAL specialist drug/substance-misuse service for same-day assessment and safe continuation of OST (using local fast-track/transfer arrangements), rather than managing it as a routine GP prescription

Provides HARM-REDUCTION safety-netting while continuity is arranged: the risks of relapse and overdose (especially with lost tolerance), advice not to top up from illicit sources, and naloxone provision/availability
Takes the RELAPSE RISK and the patient’s wider stability (work, family, recovery) seriously as part of the urgency, and documents the verification/bridging steps
Treats him with RESPECT and dignity — not suspicion-as-dismissal — hears the fear of withdrawal/relapse and of being judged, and reassures he will not be abandoned
Holds the safety boundary (no blind script) WITHOUT rupturing trust, framing verification/urgent routing as the way he gets his treatment safely and fast

Safety-nets and follows up: the verification + same-day drug-service route confirmed, harm-reduction/overdose advice and naloxone, what to do meanwhile, and follow-up to ensure continuity happened — safe, verified bridging, treating him as a person

worked.txt: "Thank you for ringing, and for being upfront — you’ve done exactly the right thing, and I’m going to take this seriously and help you. I can hear you’re frightened of withdrawal and, more than that, of slipping back when you’ve worked hard to be stable. I’m not going to judge you or leave you stuck."

worked.lbl: Why I can’t just write it
worked.txt: "Here’s the honest reason I can’t simply write a methadone script down the phone today: methadone is genuinely dangerous if the dose isn’t confirmed — it’s long-acting and the safety margin is narrow, and if anything about the dose or your tolerance were off, it could be life-threatening. That’s not me doubting you; it’s me keeping you safe. So we do it the safe, fast way instead."

"What I’m going to do right now is contact your previous drug service and pharmacy to confirm your dose and when you last picked up, and get you straight in to the local drug team — they can usually see transfers the same day and continue your script safely. That’s the proper, quick way to keep you covered."

"While I sort that, a couple of important things: please don’t top up from anywhere else to get through — that’s where the real danger is. If you’ve got naloxone, keep it to hand; if not, the drug service will sort that. And tell me — are you safe right now, anything else going on I should know?"

"I want to be really clear: you are not being fobbed off and you’re not being left to relapse. The opposite — I’m treating this as urgent because your stability matters. We’re going to get your treatment continued safely, today if at all possible."

"I’ll ring the drug service and your old pharmacy now and call you straight back with the plan and where to go. If you start feeling really unwell, or you’re ever at risk of overdose, that’s 999. You rang asking me to write a script; what I’m doing is the safer thing — getting you continued properly and fast, and standing by you while I do it."

f.learning: A new patient asking for urgent methadone continuation is a safe-bridging dilemma. Prescribing methadone BLIND on an unverified phone request is dangerous — methadone has a narrow safety margin and long half-life, and an unverified/excessive dose, or one given to someone who has lost tolerance after a gap, can be fatal — so a GP should NOT issue a methadone script on an unverified request. But the opposite failure, refusing and abandoning him to withdrawal and relapse, is also unsafe and unkind. The safe path is verified, urgent continuity: contact his previous drug service/prescriber and pharmacy to confirm dose/regimen/last pick-up, and route him rapidly to the local specialist drug service for same-day assessment and safe continuation (using transfer fast-tracks), with harm-reduction safety-netting (relapse/overdose risk, don’t top up illicitly, naloxone). The examinable hidden agenda is genuine fear of withdrawal and, more, of relapse and losing hard-won stability, plus shame and expectation of being judged; treat him with respect not suspicion, take the relapse risk seriously, hold the no-blind-script boundary without rupturing trust, and reassure he won’t be abandoned — safe continuity, fast.

knowledge.guideline: DHSC Drug misuse and dependence: UK guidelines on clinical management (2017, the “Orange Book”) · NICE TA114 (methadone and buprenorphine for opioid dependence, 2007) · BNF · Human Medicines (Amendment) Regulations 2015 (naloxone)
knowledge.summary: Never prescribe methadone blind, and never simply refuse. Verify the dose and last dispensing with the previous prescriber and pharmacy, and get him to the local drug service urgently for safe continuation, with harm-reduction advice meanwhile.

points.t: Methadone has a long and variable half-life and a narrow margin between a therapeutic and a fatal dose. An unverified dose, a duplicate prescription, or a dose given after tolerance has fallen during a gap can cause fatal respiratory depression. Deaths cluster around starting and transfer.

Orange Book (2017): before continuing opioid substitution therapy for someone new, confirm the prescriber, dose, supervision arrangements and date of last dispensing with the previous prescriber and pharmacy, and make sure the previous prescription is cancelled to avoid double prescribing. Get the patient’s consent to share information.

Contact the local drug and alcohol service the same day; most have arrangements for patients transferring in. Any bridging supply from the practice should follow written confirmation from the previous prescriber, specialist advice, local shared-care arrangements and daily supervised consumption; doses per BNF and the specialist.

If doses have been missed, tolerance may fall within days, so a restart needs clinical reassessment. Relapse to illicit opioids, especially on top of methadone or with alcohol or benzodiazepines, carries a high overdose risk.
Since the Human Medicines (Amendment) Regulations 2015, drug services can supply naloxone without a prescription. Check whether he has a kit and that someone near him knows how to use it.

Signs of overdose (pinpoint pupils, drowsiness, slow or noisy breathing, unresponsiveness): 999 and naloxone if available. Withdrawal is very unpleasant but rarely dangerous in itself; the danger lies in using on top.

dg.d: Identity and address check; open question; acknowledges urgency without agreeing to a blind script.
Recent move, recovery and stability, support nearby, previous experiences of stigma.
Verification with previous prescriber and pharmacy; last dose and missed doses; supervision; concurrent substances.
Genuine continuity need versus unverified dose, lost tolerance, or a risk of duplicate prescriptions.
Overdose risk from topping up or lost tolerance; alcohol and benzodiazepines; immediate safety and self-harm checked.
Opioid dependence on OST needing verified, urgent continuity, stated clearly to him.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

cm.d: No blind script; same-day verification; urgent routing to the local drug service; supervised bridge only after confirmation and specialist advice.
Naloxone replacement, support person, advice against using on top or with alcohol or sedatives.
Callback within the hour; 999 for overdose signs; what to do if withdrawal worsens; documents the steps.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan
cm.d: Tailored the plan to the patient’s circumstances, beliefs and practical barriers rather than giving a generic plan.

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options
cm.d: Explained the benefits and risks of the options clearly, as concrete terms or numbers where possible.
Acknowledged autonomy, capacity, confidentiality, safeguarding and any fitness-to-drive/work or duty-of-care implications relevant to this case.
Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

ro.d: Follows “I’m scared I’ll end up using” and “doctors look at me like I’m just an addict”.
Idea (GP writes a script); concerns (withdrawal, relapse, losing stability, judgement); expectation (60 ml today).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — "I'm scared I'll end up using again." And losing contact with your daughter — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Hello, is that Danny Boyd? It’s Dr Ahmed from the surgery. Can you confirm your date of birth and your new address for me? Thanks. I understand this is urgent. Tell me what’s going on.
model.why: Identity check for a new patient, then an open question

model.text: I’ve just moved here, registered last week. I’m on methadone, 60 ml a day, and my script runs out today. If I don’t get it I’ll be climbing the walls tonight, and honestly I’m scared I’ll end up using again. I just need you to write me a script. Please.

Thank you for ringing and for being so upfront. I’m taking this seriously, and I’m going to help you get your treatment continued. I need to ask a few things so we do it safely and quickly. Is that okay?
model.why: Respect and urgency from the first sentence

model.text: Yeah. Just, please don’t fob me off.
Who has been prescribing your methadone, and which pharmacy were you collecting from? Do you have their names or numbers?
model.why: Gathers what is needed to verify

model.text: My old drug service. I’ve got my keyworker’s number and the chemist’s in my phone.
That’s really helpful. Is it alright with you if I contact them to confirm your dose and when you last collected?
Yes, of course.
When did you last take a dose, and have you missed any over the move?
Yesterday morning was the last one. I haven’t missed any before that.
Were you collecting daily and taking it at the pharmacy, or taking some home? And are you using anything else at the moment: heroin, other tablets, alcohol?
model.why: Establishes supervision and concurrent use (overdose risk)

model.text: Supervised most days. Nothing else, I’ve been clean a good while. That’s why I’m so scared.
You said you’re scared. Tell me more about that.
I’ve worked hard to get stable. If I go into withdrawal, I know what I’ll do. And every time I’ve moved, doctors look at me like I’m just an addict after drugs.
That sounds really hard, and I’m sorry that’s been your experience. You’ve done well to get stable, and my job today is to protect that, not judge it. What were you hoping I could do?
model.why: Validates the fear of judgement and elicits expectations

model.text: Just write it. Sixty mil. Today.

I’ll be honest about why I can’t just write it right now. Methadone stays in the body a long time and the gap between a safe dose and a dangerous one is narrow. If anything about the dose or your tolerance were different from what we think, or two prescriptions overlapped, it could be life-threatening. That’s not me doubting you. It’s the rule I’d follow for anyone, to keep them alive.
model.why: Explains the no-blind-script boundary with reasons, not suspicion

model.text: So I’m stuck, then.

No, you’re not. Here’s what I’ll do now: ring your keyworker and your old pharmacy to confirm your dose and last pick-up and cancel the old script, then ring the local drug service. They see people transferring in, often the same day, and they can continue your methadone safely.
model.why: Verification plus urgent routing to the specialist service

model.text: And if they can’t see me today?

Then once your old service confirms everything in writing, I’ll speak to the local specialists about a short bridging supply, collected and taken at a pharmacy each day, until they take over. Either way, I’m not leaving this until there’s a plan for tonight.
model.why: Contingency for a verified, supervised bridge with specialist input

model.text: While I sort that, two important things. Please don’t use anything on top to get through. If your tolerance has dropped even a little, that’s where overdoses happen. Do you have a naloxone kit?
model.why: Harm reduction: no topping up, naloxone

model.text: I had one. I don’t know where it is after the move.
I’ll ask the drug service to give you a new one, and it’s worth showing someone close to you how to use it. Is there anyone with you, or anyone who could be?
model.why: Naloxone provision and support network without assuming details

model.text: Yeah, there’s someone I can call.
Good. One more question, because I ask everyone in this situation: are you having any thoughts of harming yourself?
No. I just want to stay on track.

I’ll call you back within the hour with where to go and when. Keep your phone on. If you or anyone sees you very drowsy, with slow or noisy breathing, that’s 999 straight away. And if withdrawal gets very bad before I ring back, call the surgery, don’t use.
model.why: Timed callback, overdose safety-net and interim plan

model.text: Okay. Within the hour.
Can you tell me what happens next, so we’re both clear?
You ring my old service and chemist, then the local drug team. You call me back. I don’t use anything, and I get a new naloxone kit.
Exactly. You did the right thing ringing us. Speak soon.

social.t: Moving area, new services and gaps in treatment are high-risk times for relapse and overdose. Continuity of OST is itself protective.
People on OST often describe being treated as “just an addict”. A respectful, urgent response keeps them engaged.

legal.t: Methadone is a Schedule 2 controlled drug. Prescriptions must meet CD requirements; instalment dispensing and supervised consumption are specified on the prescription.

DVLA: drug dependence, including treatment on an OST programme, must be declared; licensing may continue on a stable supervised programme subject to assessment. Methadone is on the drug-driving specified list (Road Traffic Act 1988 section 5A), with a medical defence if taken as prescribed and not impaired.
GMC Confidentiality (2017): obtain his consent before contacting the previous service and pharmacy, and record it.

professional.t: GMC Good practice in prescribing and managing medicines and devices (2021): prescribe controlled drugs only with adequate knowledge of the patient’s health and current medicines. Verification is a professional duty, not distrust.
Take-home methadone can be fatal to a child. If children are ever in the home, discuss locked storage.
Record who was contacted, what was confirmed, the plan agreed with the drug service, and the callback.

community.t: The local drug and alcohol service (self-referral usually possible), community pharmacy naloxone schemes where available, and peer-support groups such as Narcotics Anonymous.

redFlags: Unverified dose, prescriber or last dispensing date
Missed doses (reduced tolerance) or using other opioids, alcohol or benzodiazepines
Thoughts of self-harm; no naloxone; alone after the move
psychosocial: Recent move and loss of his usual services
Pride in recovery and fear of losing it
Past experiences of being judged by doctors
ice: Idea: the GP can write a methadone script today
Concern: withdrawal tonight, relapse, and being dismissed as “just an addict”

playbook.diagnosis: “You’re on a treatment that’s keeping you stable, and we need to continue it without a gap. Because methadone is dangerous if the dose isn’t confirmed, the safe and fast way is to verify it now and get you seen by the local drug team.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Methadone is like a key cut to fit one lock. If I cut it from memory and it’s slightly wrong, it can do real harm. Your old service has the exact pattern, so I’ll get it from them today.”

management.reflectIce: “You’re frightened of losing everything you’ve worked for. That’s exactly why I’m treating this as urgent, and why I want to do it safely.”
management.psychosocial: Respond to past stigma directly, involve a support person, and give him a clear timed plan so he isn’t left waiting.
sharedPlan: Consent obtained; verify dose and last dispensing with previous prescriber and pharmacy; ensure the old prescription is cancelled
Same-day contact with the local drug service for transfer; supervised bridge only after written confirmation and specialist advice
Harm reduction: no using on top, avoid alcohol and sedatives, replacement naloxone
safetyNet: Overdose signs (very drowsy, slow or noisy breathing, unresponsive): 999 and naloxone

pitfalls.intro: This station tests a safety boundary held with compassion. Candidates fail by prescribing on trust, by refusing without acting, or by letting suspicion leak into their language.

items.fail: Issuing a methadone prescription on the patient’s reported dose.
items.why: An unverified dose, lost tolerance or double prescribing can be fatal. This is a critical safety fail.
items.fix: Verify with the previous prescriber and pharmacy and involve the local drug service first.

items.fail: Refusing and telling him to sort it out with his old service.
items.why: Abandonment leads to withdrawal and relapse, with a high overdose risk. Refusal without action is also unsafe.
items.fix: Take on the verification and routing yourself, with a timed callback.

items.fail: Not asking about missed doses or other substances.
items.why: These determine tolerance and overdose risk and change what the specialist can safely prescribe.
items.fix: Ask about the last dose, any gaps, and heroin, tablets or alcohol.

items.fail: Questioning whether he is really on methadone.
items.why: Suspicion confirms his experience of stigma and damages engagement.
items.fix: Frame verification as a universal safety rule: “I’d do this for anyone.”

items.why: The interim period is when overdose risk peaks.
items.fix: Advise against using on top, check naloxone, and name the signs of overdose.

items.fail: Ending with “someone will be in touch”.
items.why: An open-ended plan for an urgent problem leaves him alone tonight.
items.fix: “I’ll ring you back within the hour with where to go.”

timeMap.d: Confirm identity and address. He asks for a script today and fears relapse. Show you are taking it seriously.
Previous prescriber and pharmacy, consent to contact, last dose, missed doses, supervision, other substances.
Relapse fear, hard-won stability, past experiences of being judged. What he hopes you’ll do.
Why not a blind script. Verify now, cancel the old prescription, local drug service today, supervised bridge only after confirmation. Harm reduction and naloxone.
Callback within the hour, overdose signs and 999, no using on top. Teach-back.

wordPics.fail: Writes a methadone prescription on his word; or refuses and tells him to contact his old service himself; treats him with suspicion; no harm-reduction advice; no callback.
wordPics.pass: Declines a blind script with a reason; takes details to verify; refers to the local drug service urgently; mentions overdose risk and naloxone; arranges to call back.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: responds to the stigma he describes; gets consent to share information; asks about missed doses and other substances; ensures the old prescription is cancelled; offers a supervised bridge after verification; timed callback and teach-back.

avoid.dont: “We don’t prescribe methadone here. You’ll need to sort it with your old service.”
avoid.instead: “I’m going to contact your old service and the local team now and ring you back with a plan for tonight.”
avoid.why: Refusal without action abandons him to withdrawal and relapse, which is unsafe.

avoid.dont: “How do I know you’re really on 60 ml?”
avoid.instead: “I check this for anyone, because methadone is dangerous if the dose isn’t confirmed.”
avoid.why: Suspicion confirms his fear of judgement; a universal safety rule does not.

avoid.dont: “I’ll write you three days to tide you over.”
avoid.instead: “Once your old service confirms the dose, we’ll arrange a supervised supply with the specialists.”
avoid.why: An unverified supply risks fatal overdose or double prescribing.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: DHSC Drug misuse and dependence: UK guidelines on clinical management (2017, the “Orange Book”) · NICE TA114 (methadone and buprenorphine for opioid dependence, 2007) · BNF · Human Medicines (Amendment) Regulations 2015 (naloxone)
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: Never prescribe methadone blind, and never simply refuse. Verify the dose and last dispensing with the previous prescriber and pharmacy, and get him to the local drug service urgently for safe continuation, with harm-reduction advice meanwhile.

points.t: Methadone has a long and variable half-life and a narrow margin between a therapeutic and a fatal dose. An unverified dose, a duplicate prescription, or a dose given after tolerance has fallen during a gap can cause fatal respiratory depression. Deaths cluster around starting and transfer.

Orange Book (2017): before continuing opioid substitution therapy for someone new, confirm the prescriber, dose, supervision arrangements and date of last dispensing with the previous prescriber and pharmacy, and make sure the previous prescription is cancelled to avoid double prescribing. Get the patient’s consent to share information.

Contact the local drug and alcohol service the same day; most have arrangements for patients transferring in. Any bridging supply from the practice should follow written confirmation from the previous prescriber, specialist advice, local shared-care arrangements and daily supervised consumption; doses per BNF and the specialist.

If doses have been missed, tolerance may fall within days, so a restart needs clinical reassessment. Relapse to illicit opioids, especially on top of methadone or with alcohol or benzodiazepines, carries a high overdose risk.
Since the Human Medicines (Amendment) Regulations 2015, drug services can supply naloxone without a prescription. Check whether he has a kit and that someone near him knows how to use it.

Signs of overdose (pinpoint pupils, drowsiness, slow or noisy breathing, unresponsiveness): 999 and naloxone if available. Withdrawal is very unpleasant but rarely dangerous in itself; the danger lies in using on top.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Identity and address check; open question; acknowledges urgency without agreeing to a blind script.
Recent move, recovery and stability, support nearby, previous experiences of stigma.
Follows “I’m scared I’ll end up using” and “doctors look at me like I’m just an addict”.
Idea (GP writes a script); concerns (withdrawal, relapse, losing stability, judgement); expectation (60 ml today).
Verification with previous prescriber and pharmacy; last dose and missed doses; supervision; concurrent substances.
Genuine continuity need versus unverified dose, lost tolerance, or a risk of duplicate prescriptions.
Overdose risk from topping up or lost tolerance; alcohol and benzodiazepines; immediate safety and self-harm checked.
Opioid dependence on OST needing verified, urgent continuity, stated clearly to him.
No blind script; same-day verification; urgent routing to the local drug service; supervised bridge only after confirmation and specialist advice.
Naloxone replacement, support person, advice against using on top or with alcohol or sedatives.
Callback within the hour; 999 for overdose signs; what to do if withdrawal worsens; documents the steps.

social.t: Moving area, new services and gaps in treatment are high-risk times for relapse and overdose. Continuity of OST is itself protective.
People on OST often describe being treated as “just an addict”. A respectful, urgent response keeps them engaged.

legal.t: Methadone is a Schedule 2 controlled drug. Prescriptions must meet CD requirements; instalment dispensing and supervised consumption are specified on the prescription.

DVLA: drug dependence, including treatment on an OST programme, must be declared; licensing may continue on a stable supervised programme subject to assessment. Methadone is on the drug-driving specified list (Road Traffic Act 1988 section 5A), with a medical defence if taken as prescribed and not impaired.
GMC Confidentiality (2017): obtain his consent before contacting the previous service and pharmacy, and record it.

professional.t: GMC Good practice in prescribing and managing medicines and devices (2021): prescribe controlled drugs only with adequate knowledge of the patient’s health and current medicines. Verification is a professional duty, not distrust.
Take-home methadone can be fatal to a child. If children are ever in the home, discuss locked storage.
Record who was contacted, what was confirmed, the plan agreed with the drug service, and the callback.

community.t: The local drug and alcohol service (self-referral usually possible), community pharmacy naloxone schemes where available, and peer-support groups such as Narcotics Anonymous.

redFlags: Unverified dose, prescriber or last dispensing date
Missed doses (reduced tolerance) or using other opioids, alcohol or benzodiazepines
Thoughts of self-harm; no naloxone; alone after the move
psychosocial: Recent move and loss of his usual services
Pride in recovery and fear of losing it
Past experiences of being judged by doctors
ice: Idea: the GP can write a methadone script today
Concern: withdrawal tonight, relapse, and being dismissed as “just an addict”

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: “You’re on a treatment that’s keeping you stable, and we need to continue it without a gap. Because methadone is dangerous if the dose isn’t confirmed, the safe and fast way is to verify it now and get you seen by the local drug team.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Methadone is like a key cut to fit one lock. If I cut it from memory and it’s slightly wrong, it can do real harm. Your old service has the exact pattern, so I’ll get it from them today.”

management.reflectIce: “You’re frightened of losing everything you’ve worked for. That’s exactly why I’m treating this as urgent, and why I want to do it safely.”
management.psychosocial: Respond to past stigma directly, involve a support person, and give him a clear timed plan so he isn’t left waiting.
sharedPlan: Consent obtained; verify dose and last dispensing with previous prescriber and pharmacy; ensure the old prescription is cancelled
Same-day contact with the local drug service for transfer; supervised bridge only after written confirmation and specialist advice
Harm reduction: no using on top, avoid alcohol and sedatives, replacement naloxone
safetyNet: Overdose signs (very drowsy, slow or noisy breathing, unresponsive): 999 and naloxone

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station tests a safety boundary held with compassion. Candidates fail by prescribing on trust, by refusing without acting, or by letting suspicion leak into their language.

items.fail: Issuing a methadone prescription on the patient’s reported dose.
items.why: An unverified dose, lost tolerance or double prescribing can be fatal. This is a critical safety fail.
items.fix: Verify with the previous prescriber and pharmacy and involve the local drug service first.

items.fail: Refusing and telling him to sort it out with his old service.
items.why: Abandonment leads to withdrawal and relapse, with a high overdose risk. Refusal without action is also unsafe.
items.fix: Take on the verification and routing yourself, with a timed callback.

items.fail: Not asking about missed doses or other substances.
items.why: These determine tolerance and overdose risk and change what the specialist can safely prescribe.
items.fix: Ask about the last dose, any gaps, and heroin, tablets or alcohol.

items.fail: Questioning whether he is really on methadone.
items.why: Suspicion confirms his experience of stigma and damages engagement.
items.fix: Frame verification as a universal safety rule: “I’d do this for anyone.”

items.why: The interim period is when overdose risk peaks.
items.fix: Advise against using on top, check naloxone, and name the signs of overdose.

items.fail: Ending with “someone will be in touch”.
items.why: An open-ended plan for an urgent problem leaves him alone tonight.
items.fix: “I’ll ring you back within the hour with where to go.”
